segments.text: Take a look at this text interface.
When an AI generates an answer,
it builds it one token at a time.
To fill in the blank after you could name him,
the model calculates a probability
for every potential word that could come next.
Here, the name spot sits at the top of the list.
But the AI doesn't automatically pick
the highest probability token.
To understand why it passes up its top choice,
we have to look at two distinct concepts,
sampling and temperature.
A 22% probability simply means
that if the odds stay exactly the same,
the AI would pick spot about 22 times out of 100 tries, on average.
This process of drawing a token based on its underlying odds
is called sampling.
This graphic breaks down how those probabilities work in practice.
Notice that the percentages on the left
remain fixed across all attempts.
What you are seeing on the right is not a sequence of words.
These are five independent alternate reality simulations
for filling that single blank space.
When we run the draw five separate times with the same odds,
we get pick one, max, pick two, spot, pick three,
buddy, pick four, rex, and pick five, max.
Spot had the undisputed highest probability at 22%,
yet it was only drawn once in this set.
These five picks represent just one possible set of outcomes.
Running another five draws would yield a completely different group of names.
Having the mathematically best chance is never an absolute guarantee of selection.
If the AI chose the most likely token every single time,
its answers would become highly repetitive.
By giving lower probability tokens a legitimate chance to win the draw,
the model injects variety into its responses.
Because every single token chosen establishes the context for the next calculation,
a single alternative choice completely redirects the rest of the sentence.
The mechanism that controls this variety is called temperature.
It is a setting that dictates whether probabilities are tightly concentrated
or widely spread out.
For typical users in chat applications,
this temperature setting is already configured behind the scenes.
This table shows how temperature manipulates the distribution curve.
We start with the baseline odds calculated from the training data and current context,
anchoring on spot at 22%.
When you lower the temperature, it takes those exact same starting odds
and concentrates them heavily onto the most likely candidates.
Spot's chances surge from 22% to 36%,
while the odds for less likely options shrink.
Raising the temperature does the opposite.
It flattens the curve, spreading the baseline probabilities much more evenly across the vocabulary.
Spot's dominance drops down to 16%,
granting lower ranked names a much better chance of being sampled during the draw.
Temperature does not invent new words.
It reshapes how safely or creatively the AI samples from its existing options.
Look at the journey of a single top token across these three states.
Spot moves from a 22% baseline to a 36% concentrated peak
down to a 16% widespread.
These specific probabilities are illustrative.
The vast amount of remaining vocabulary odds are condensed here into the other category.
While temperature aggressively reshapes the selection probabilities,
it absolutely does not alter the underlying weights the model learned during its training.
The best chance is in a guarantee.
Different choices, same learned weights.
